analysis.headline: Introduced February 4, 2025 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred the same day to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap the interest rate on any credit card at 10% per year, counting all finance charges toward that limit, and would stop lenders from using fees to get around the cap. If a lender knowingly charges more, it forfeits all the interest on the debt, and a cardholder could sue to get back interest, finance charges, or fees paid in the previous two years. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission could also enforce the cap under the Truth in Lending Act, and state laws protecting consumers more would still apply. The cap is temporary — it ends on January 1, 2031 unless Congress extends it.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit cardholders who carry a balance, especially those paying interest rates well above 10% — the cap would directly lower what they owe each month. Any cardholder overcharged could also sue to recover the interest, finance charges, or fees they paid in the prior two years [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit cards at 10%, inclusive of all finance charges.
Blocks evasion: fees that don't count as finance charges cannot be used to get around the cap, and their total cannot exceed the total finance charges assessed.

If a lender knowingly charges above the cap, it forfeits the entire interest on the debt, and the cardholder can sue within two years to recover the full amount of interest, finance charges, or fees paid.
Makes violations enforceable as civil violations under the Truth in Lending Act, which the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission police.
Does not override state laws that give consumers stronger protections.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuing banks and finance companies. Interest and fee income is the core of their card business; a 10% cap would cut the rates most of them charge far below current levels, and knowing violators would forfeit all interest on the affected debt [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The 10% cap is flat — it applies to every cardholder regardless of credit risk. Lenders that cannot charge higher rates to borrowers with weaker credit histories may respond the way they do under other rate caps: denying cards, lowering credit limits, or tightening approval, which shrinks access to credit for the riskier borrowers the cap most aims to help. (Mechanism of rate caps generally; the bill imposes the cap on all card APRs with no risk-based exception [S3].)

Because fees are folded into the cap and capped relative to finance charges [S3], issuers would have limited ways to recover costs, so the adjustment would likely come through credit availability and card terms rather than price.
The cap sunsets on January 1, 2031, so any relief is temporary unless Congress acts again.

The harshest penalty — forfeiting all interest on the debt — applies only to violations committed knowingly, so unintentional overcharges fall back on a two-year private right of action and ordinary Truth in Lending Act remedies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to understand: cardholders carrying balances at high rates would owe far less interest, and those overcharged could claw back what they paid. The cost falls on card-issuing banks. The honest tradeoff — the one economists of most stripes raise about binding rate caps — is that lenders who cannot price for risk tend to restrict who gets credit at all, so some high-risk borrowers could lose access to cards rather than gain cheaper ones. The design softens this only partially: the bill is temporary (ending in 2031), keeps stronger state protections in place, and builds in private enforcement. It is a straightforward, well-intentioned cap whose main open question is not intent but whether lenders' response would leave the riskiest borrowers worse off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on February 4, 2025, together with Senator Josh Hawley.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Three senators cosponsored the bill: one Republican and two Democrats.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

key_actors.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the 10 Percent Credit Card Interest Rate Cap Act on February 4, 2025.

key_actors.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
key_actors.role: Original cosponsor; joined Sanders in introducing the bill
key_actors.what_they_did: Put his name on the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

key_actors.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 4, 2025 and has taken no further action on it, leaving it without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

analysis.trajectory: With only three cosponsors and no committee activity since its February 2025 referral, the bill is very likely to remain in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or markup, as most credit card rate-cap bills have. Advancing would require the committee chair to schedule action and Senate leadership to bring it to the floor; neither is indicated by the record so far.
